title: The rope and the snake
hookLine: a coil lies across the garden path at dusk, and the Vivekachudamani asks what happens when someone brings a lamp
carry: a rope taken for a snake: the self mistaken

lines: A COIL ON THE PATH AT DUSK.
cards: A coil lies across the garden path at dusk. Someone walking home stops dead. It's long, it's curved, it might have moved.
The heart pounds, the breath goes short, and they're already backing toward the gate. Then a neighbor steps out with a lamp. It's a rope, left lying there after somebody tied up the gate.
Nothing on the path has changed. The rope was a rope the whole time. But the fear was real, and so was the step backward.
The Vivekachudamani puts that small scene to work.

teach.h: A ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.
teach.b: When the teacher wants to show the student what has gone wrong, one picture he reaches for is the rope and the snake. In paraphrase: through not knowing, a rope is taken for a snake, and fear follows.
Through not knowing, the Self is taken for the body, the mind, the restless one who worries, and suffering follows.

teach.h: ADHYASA: ONE THING LAID ON ANOTHER.
teach.b: The teaching's name for that mistake is adhyasa, superimposition: laying one thing on top of another. The snake is laid on the rope. The small, anxious I is laid on the Self.
Now notice what the cure is not.
Nobody kills the snake. Nobody runs for a stick, or better boots, or a long practice of being brave around snakes. That would be fighting something that isn't there.
The cure is a lamp. Light falls on the rope, and the snake is simply gone, as long as the light stays on. That's jnana on this path: not collecting facts, but knowing that removes a mistake.

And the rope never needed fixing. On this reading, the Self was never actually bound; the binding belonged to the seeing. That's why, two days ago, the teacher insisted the student look for themselves.
A lamp held by someone else helps. But the snake only disappears for the one whose own eyes see the rope.

how: In Advaita teaching, the rope taken for a snake is an image used to explain adhyasa: the Self mistaken for the body and mind, set right by knowing rather than by effort.

o: a large store of facts gathered from holy books
a brave fight against the snake in the dark
knowing that clears a mistake, like light on a rope

games.q: the rope and the snake — tap the pairs.
p: what fear lays on the rope
jnana, knowing that removes a mistake
laying one thing on top of another

s: on this path, the cure for the snake is to fight it bravely
nobody kills the snake. the cure is light: once the rope is seen, the snake is simply gone.
in the picture, the rope itself never changes
only the seeing changes, and with it the snake is gone.
jnana here means knowing a great many facts
in this teaching it means the seeing that removes a mistake, like a lamp on a rope.

games.q: you're the student. the teacher says the snake was never there. what do you ask next?
o: then how do I kill it?
then why does my heart still pound?
then what do I need to see for myself?
games.why: the teaching points to light, not a fight: the snake only goes for the one whose own eyes see the rope.

practice: Let the breath find its own pace. Before long a thought will arrive dressed as a fact about you: I'm tired, I'm behind, I'm not good at this.
Don't argue with it or chase it off; hold a small lamp to it, and notice that it's a thought, appearing, and what is aware of it appearing. It may stay or go; either way, keep the light on.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing, on the path of knowing: not a pile of facts, but the seeing that turns the snake back into a rope.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: adhyasa, superimposition, laying one thing on top of another, like a snake on a rope.

carryVoice: Your line: a rope taken for a snake, the self mistaken. The snake was never there to fight. Good to see you today.

sources.work: Shankara's commentary on the Brahma Sutras (paraphrased)
